quote: If P ≠ NP and the universe has no source of exponential computing power, then there are evidential updates too difficult for even a superintelligence to compute
content: The point is right but the complexity theory is off. Exact Bayesian inference is a counting problem. Computing posterior probabilities in Bayesian networks is #P-hard (Roth 1996), and even approximating them within fixed bounds is NP-hard (Cooper 1990; Dagum & Luby 1993). P ≠ NP is the conjecture behind the approximation result. Exact inference would not obviously become tractable even if P = NP. That the laws of probability are "too expensive" is also a reason to doubt they are the right standard for agents with limited computation, which the essay doesn't consider.

quote: To be specific, I would advise, in most cases, against using non-numerical procedures to create what appear to be numerical probabilities. Numbers should come from numbers.
content: The largest test of this advice came out against it. In the Good Judgment Project, forecasters produced numerical probabilities for geopolitical questions by judgment alone, with no model or dataset to derive them from. The best of them were well calibrated and highly accurate (Mellers et al. 2014). Rounding their forecasts to coarser categories measurably reduced accuracy, so the fine numerical distinctions carried real information (Friedman et al. 2018). Numbers produced by non-numerical judgment turned out to beat the words the essay recommends.

quote: But the speaker actually purported to assign a probability of at least 1 in 1,000 that the theory, model, or calculations in the LHC paper were wrong
content: The talk became Ord, Hillerbrand & Sandberg (2010), and the paper grounds its numbers in empirical rates: how often published scientific work contains errors or is retracted, and how often established theories and calculations have turned out wrong. Those are numbers from numbers, the method this essay recommends, so "pulled out of thin air" misdescribes the target. The paper's core argument is that the probability a safety argument is flawed puts a floor under how low a risk estimate can go, and it has been widely cited in risk analysis since.

quote: I cannot be sure of this statement, of course, but it has a probability of 75%.
content: The joke, a made-up probability to mock made-up probabilities, misses that stating a number is what lets a forecast be scored. "Probably" and "maybe" can't be checked for calibration; "75%" can, across many such statements. That is why research on intelligence analysis and forecasting favors numbers. People interpret verbal probability terms with enormous variability: Beyth-Marom (1982)'s subjects read "probable" as meaning anything from roughly 25% to 90%. Numbers communicate uncertainty more accurately (Dhami & Mandel 2021).

quote: What should I do about this inconsistency? I’m not sure, but I’m certainly not going to wave a magic wand to make it go away.
content: This is the inconsistency the Allais essays forbid. There, preferences that no single coherent assignment of probabilities and utilities can represent make you a money pump, and the reader is told: "Just give up already! Intuition isn't always right!" Here the author's own incoherent credences are to be kept, on the grounds that fixing them might cost accuracy: he is more alarmed by a one-in-a-million doomsday device than by the LHC, yet won't bet at the matching odds. Both positions may be defensible, but not under the same standard, and the book applies the stricter one to other people's intuitions.
